question: Why does my dog get tired so fast in hot or humid weather?
answer: It's almost always a cooling problem, not a fitness or fuel problem. Dogs can't sweat to cool down — their main tool is panting, which works by evaporating moisture off the tongue and airways. On hot and especially HUMID days, that evaporation stops working well (the air is already saturated), so heat builds up faster than they can dump it, and they fatigue quickly to protect themselves. This is why a dog can crash after a few minutes of hard play on a muggy day but be totally fine on a cool one. The tiredness is heat management, not weakness.
source: Common Sense Dog — Heat & Exercise Safety pack

question: Does humidity matter more than temperature for dogs?
answer: Often, yes — humidity is the sneaky factor people underestimate. Because dogs cool primarily by evaporation (panting), high humidity cripples that system even when the temperature seems mild. A 70°F day at 70%+ humidity can be harder on a sprinting dog than a warmer but dry day, because the moist air can't absorb the evaporating heat. So don't judge safety by temperature alone — factor in the humidity. When it's muggy, dial the intensity down even if it doesn't feel that hot to you.
source: Common Sense Dog — Heat & Exercise Safety pack

question: My dog fades during sprints but is fine on long walks or swimming — is it heat or does he need more carbs?
answer: That pattern points squarely to heat, not fuel. Two clues give it away: (1) if he can go for an hour or two at lower intensity, his energy supply is clearly fine — a real carb/fuel deficiency would show up in endurance, not just short bursts; and (2) if he's totally fine SWIMMING, that's the giveaway, because water carries heat away from his body so cooling is no longer the bottleneck. Sprints generate the most heat the fastest, so on a warm or humid day he hits the cooling wall in minutes. Don't add carbs to fix this — his fuel is fine; it's a heat-dissipation limit. Save sprints for cooler, drier days.
source: Common Sense Dog — Heat & Exercise Safety pack

question: Do dogs need extra carbohydrates for energy and endurance?
answer: Not really — dogs convert fat to energy very efficiently, and fat is actually their preferred fuel for sustained activity, so they don't need a high-carb diet to be energetic. Endurance running dogs do great on high-fat, high-protein, low-carb diets. A small complex-carb topper (like a bit of cooked sweet potato, ~5% of calories) before genuinely intense sprint/burst work can help top off muscle glycogen, but that's fine-tuning for high-intensity athletes — not a fix for general tiredness. If your dog seems to run out of gas, look at heat, hydration, weight, and health before assuming it's a carb shortage.

question: What are the signs of heatstroke in dogs?
answer: Heatstroke is a true emergency, so know the signs: frantic or excessive panting, thick drooling, bright red or (worse) dark/bluish gums, glassy eyes, weakness, stumbling or an unsteady gait, vomiting or diarrhea, disorientation, and eventually collapse or seizures. A dog that's overheating and NOT recovering after stopping is a red alert. Normal dog temperature is about 101–102.5°F; above ~104°F is dangerous and above ~106°F is critical and life-threatening. If you see these signs, act immediately — heatstroke can damage organs and kill within minutes.

question: What should I do if my dog overheats?
answer: Act fast and cool him down, then get to a vet. Move him to shade or air conditioning, offer small amounts of cool water, and start cooling his body with COOL (not ice-cold) water — hose or pour it over his belly, groin, armpits, and paws, and use a fan to boost evaporation. Do NOT use ice or ice-cold water, which can constrict blood vessels and trap heat, or cause shock. Then take him to a vet even if he seems to bounce back, because heatstroke can cause delayed internal organ damage that isn't visible right away. Cooling first, vet immediately after — both matter.
source: Common Sense Dog — Heat & Exercise Safety pack

question: How can I exercise my dog safely in hot weather?
answer: Work with your dog's cooling limits, not against them. Exercise in the cooler parts of the day (early morning, evening) and skip midday heat; on hot or humid days, trade high-intensity sprints for steady, low-intensity activity or swimming. Always bring water and take shade breaks, and check the pavement with your hand — if it's too hot for your palm for 5 seconds, it'll burn paw pads. Watch for early fatigue and heavy panting and stop before he's in trouble. When it's muggy, remember a dog's self-imposed 'break' is smart self-preservation, not laziness — let him set the pace.
source: Common Sense Dog — Heat & Exercise Safety pack

question: Which dogs overheat most easily?
answer: Some dogs are at much higher risk and need extra caution: flat-faced (brachycephalic) breeds like Bulldogs, Pugs, and Boxers are the highest risk because their airways make panting inefficient; dark-coated and thick/double-coated dogs absorb and trap more heat; overweight dogs, seniors, puppies, and dogs with heart or breathing conditions all struggle more; and dogs that naturally 'run hot' (in TCVM terms) overheat sooner. If your dog fits any of these, be especially conservative in heat and humidity — shorter sessions, more shade and water, and lean hard on swimming as the safest hot-weather exercise.
source: Common Sense Dog — Heat & Exercise Safety pack

question: Does giving my dog water fix the heat problem?
answer: Water is essential for hydration, but it doesn't solve the cooling problem on a humid day. The limit isn't thirst — it's that panting (evaporative cooling) can't keep up when the air is already saturated with moisture. So a dog with water right there can still overheat during hard exercise in humidity, because drinking doesn't restore the evaporation his body needs to shed heat. Water plus SHADE, rest, wetting him down, and lower intensity is what actually helps. Always provide water, but don't assume it makes heavy exercise safe in the heat.
source: Common Sense Dog — Heat & Exercise Safety pack

question: Is swimming good exercise for dogs?
answer: Swimming is one of the best forms of exercise for dogs, especially in warm weather. It's low-impact (easy on joints — great for seniors, arthritic, or recovering dogs), builds strong cardiovascular fitness and muscle, and it has built-in cooling since the water carries heat away from the body — which is exactly why a dog who overheats sprinting on land can swim happily for a long time. Just supervise closely, introduce water gradually (not all dogs are natural swimmers), rinse off chlorine or salt afterward, and dry the ears to prevent infections. On hot, humid days it's the smartest workout you can offer.
source: Common Sense Dog — Heat & Exercise Safety pack
